title: When the Earth Gives Way | Francesca Billington
gist: Seventy-five years of underground iron mining has made the ground under Kiruna, Sweden sink and crack, forcing state-owned LKAB and the municipality into a two-decade relocation of the entire city center two miles east — with the scope escalating from 6,000 residents in 2004 to two-thirds of all residents within the next decade. The reporting documents how mine-life extensions are purchased with municipal displacement, how LKAB's discovery of Europe's largest known rare earth deposit raises the stakes again, and how cost-sharing between company and city was left deliberately vague.

insights.claim: Almost seventy-five years of underground ore mining has caused the surface of the earth in Kiruna to sink, collapse and crack, and in 2004 mine operator LKAB announced the city center would need to be relocated.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A worked example of the long-tail surface-liability that underground mining generates and that mine-life NPV models typically exclude.
insights.locator: Almost seventy-five years of underground ore mining

insights.claim: The original 2004 plan required about six thousand residents — a third of the population — to evacuate, with the city center, Kiruna's schools, hospitals and some one thousand places of work demolished, and historic buildings including the church transported to the new city.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Sizes the social cost attached to extending one mine — the order of magnitude to expect in comparable single-employer resource towns.
insights.locator: In 2004, the company in charge of the mine

insights.claim: Kiruna began its two-mile migration east in 2014, and the project to destroy and rebuild the central city — known as the urban or social transformation — has now been ongoing for more than two decades since the initial announcement.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Twenty-plus years and counting is the realistic timeline for mine-driven urban relocation — a benchmark against optimistic corporate schedules.
insights.locator: In 2014, Kiruna began its migration two miles east

insights.claim: The architect hired to design the new city explicitly rejected the utopian-experiment framing, calling the project crisis management in which the survival of Kiruna, its inhabitants and its economy is at stake if it goes wrong.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Frames the relocation as existential risk management rather than urban design ambition — relevant to how comparable projects should be underwritten.
insights.quote: If this project goes wrong, the survival of Kiruna, its inhabitants and its economy is at stake.

insights.claim: By August 2023 the city had entered heavy demolition because leaving the old city intact was a safety hazard, with cracks appearing in buildings and ground deformations moving further east.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Deformation is advancing, not stabilizing, meaning the affected footprint is a moving target and further liabilities are likely.

insights.claim: Four years after its initial warnings, LKAB's board approved construction of a new mine level that extended the mine's lifespan by another thirty years but required even more people to evacuate — showing mine-life extension being purchased directly with municipal displacement.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The reserve-life headline and the resettlement liability are two sides of the same board decision — read mine-extension announcements as displacement announcements.
insights.locator: Four years after its initial ominous warnings to the Council

insights.claim: Three years before the article, LKAB announced it had found Europe's largest known deposit of rare earth minerals at Kiruna — ingredients for electric car batteries and wind turbines not currently mined on the continent — with extraction threatening reindeer migration routes.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Europe's flagship answer to Chinese rare-earth dependence sits under a town already collapsing and on Indigenous herding land — permitting and social-license risk on the EU critical-minerals plan.
insights.locator: Three years ago, with the construction of New Kiruna well underway

insights.claim: Last summer LKAB announced that an additional six thousand people — now two-thirds of all residents — need to move within the next decade to accommodate the latest expansion.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The displacement scope has doubled from the original plan while the first relocation is unfinished — evidence that these liabilities compound rather than close out.
insights.locator: And then last summer LKAB announced

insights.claim: The timeline for evacuating and rebuilding changed repeatedly after LKAB's initial five-sentence letter to the Kiruna Municipal Council in 2004, leaving residents confused about both the severity of the deformations and when they would have a new city.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Chronic schedule revision is the pattern — treat stated relocation timelines from mine operators as opening bids.
insights.locator: LKAB presented its first proposal to expand Kiruna’s mine

insights.claim: LKAB agreed to cover relocation costs and the city agreed to rezone municipal land for the mine, but it remained unclear who would cover which expenses and how the two entities would work together on city planning.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: An unquantified, unallocated multi-billion liability sitting between a state-owned miner and a municipality — the kind of contingent exposure that surfaces only when the sovereign is asked to pay.
insights.locator: LKAB had agreed to cover costs related to the relocation

themes.theme: Single-employer dependence and the impossibility of refusal

insights.claim: LKAB employs about a third of Kiruna Municipality's twenty-two thousand residents, and anthropologist Elisa Maria López characterizes the city's relationship to the company as not simply dependence but an impossibility of refusal, partly because LKAB is funding construction of most buildings in the new city center.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: When the counterparty funds the town it is displacing, there is no adversarial party to negotiate compensation — a structural reason mining social costs stay under-priced.
insights.quote: To refuse this corporate relationship, either as a city or a resident, she writes, would mean to leave.
insights.locator: Today, LKAB employs about a third

insights.claim: The dependency is original to the town's design: LKAB built a model industrial city in 1910 next to the mine on land home to Indigenous Sami reindeer herders and, in exchange for local tax exemptions, paid for infrastructure including a fire station, a hospital and a church, before the Swedish government gradually bought shares until nationalizing the company in 1957.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Tax-exemption-for-infrastructure was the founding bargain, which is why the municipality has no independent fiscal capacity to fund its own relocation now.
insights.locator: As mining expanded, workers from southern Sweden resettled north

insights.claim: The core tension the reporting identifies is that the survival of a mining town depends on the life of the mine while mining is itself incompatible with living there.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The clearest statement of why resource-town social costs cannot be engineered away — they scale with the very reserve life that justifies the investment.
insights.quote: The survival of a mining town depends on the “life” of the mine, but mining is incompatible with living.
insights.locator: The survival of a mining town depends on the “life” of the mine

insights.claim: Public services degraded during the transition: Kiruna's hospital had no maternity ward and no longer performed surgeries, and on the author's flight north an emergency landing was made at Lulea because it was better to be sick there.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Service collapse during a decades-long rebuild is the hidden cost that drives out the working-age population the new city is supposed to attract.
insights.locator: I asked him about the hospital, which did not currently have a maternity ward

insights.claim: Kiruna hosts the largest underground iron ore mine in the world, and every morning between 1:15 and 1:45 it begins blasting, sending what feel like tiny earthquakes through parts of the city while a mile east nothing is felt.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The damage gradient is steep and local, which is what makes a two-mile city move a viable engineering answer at all.
insights.locator: Every morning between 1:15 and 1:45

insights.claim: LKAB says it mines enough iron ore to build six and a half Eiffel Towers every day, with four trains of pellets arriving at the port of Luleå daily.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Throughput of this scale is why the Swedish state tolerates relocating a city — the output is strategically material to European steel supply.
insights.locator: LKAB says that it mines enough iron ore

insights.claim: The extraction method is sub-level caving, in which a remote-controlled drilling rig cuts long holes upward into the ore body and fills them with explosives detonated once a day, with ore then crushed and rolled with water and chemical additives into highly concentrated pellets.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Sub-level caving is the specific technique that makes surface subsidence unavoidable — a diagnostic for which mines carry this class of liability.
insights.locator: showed us a retired yellow mining truck

insights.claim: Environmental spillover beyond subsidence is documented, with the small lake Luossajärvi near the mine now partially drained and polluted with sulphate and nitrate.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Water impacts sit alongside ground deformation as a second unpriced liability class at long-life underground operations.
insights.locator: After a short bus drive out of the old city

themes.theme: Managing the narrative and the damage

insights.claim: LKAB, the Swedish state and Kiruna's municipal council chairman Mats Taaveniku are marketing the move as an economic and cultural upgrade, with Taaveniku targeting population growth to twenty-five thousand people by 2030.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A growth target set against ongoing forced displacement and service loss is the metric to test whether relocation narratives ever hold up.
insights.quote: “If you ever thought about moving to Kiruna, now is the right time,”
insights.locator: LKAB, the state, and Kiruna’s chairman of the municipal council

insights.claim: Physical damage is being managed with visible temporary fixes rather than repair: duct tape over a split windowsill at the old high school, columns wrapped in steel slabs as reinforcement, plastic covers over floor cracks, and LKAB employees leaving coded annotations along the cracks.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Concealment-grade maintenance in a building slated for demolition is what interim risk management looks like in practice — a signal of how long the tail runs.
insights.locator: Timo led us down a dark hallway toward his office

insights.claim: Demolition serves a psychological function by letting residents stop shuttling back and forth between the old and new cities, between past and future.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The rationale for destroying still-standing assets is behavioral, not structural — a cost driver that engineering assessments will miss.
insights.quote: “It’s not the end of the world. It’s way beyond,”
insights.locator: Demolition has a psychological function too

insights.claim: The urgency is driven by the physical advance of the damage, with the council chairman insisting on immediate action because the crack line moves very fast.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The deformation front, not political timelines, sets the schedule — deadlines here are geological and cannot be renegotiated.
insights.quote: “We can’t wait anymore,” Taaveniku continued, forcefully. “This crack line moves very fast.”
insights.locator: Many things seemed to be underway “right now.”

insights.claim: New Kiruna is experienced as a downgrade despite the upgrade marketing: buildings and apartments painted gray rather than the bright colors of the old town, narrow streets that gesture at quaintness but read as impersonal and depressing, routes interrupted by closures and fences, and residents reporting the new city feels colder and windier.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Purpose-built replacement towns underdeliver on livability, which undermines the retention assumptions that justify the relocation spend.
insights.locator: Most homes in Old Kiruna had been painted bright colors

insights.claim: The 670-ton Kiruna church was moved in August 2025 on a 224-wheel trailer after contractors widened roads, removed lampposts and road signs, and ran tests with weighted trailers, driving it during daylight hours over two days.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Concrete cost anchor for the heritage-preservation line item that mine relocations must fund.
insights.locator: In August 2025, two years after I left Kiruna

insights.claim: Kiruna is not unique: a Minnesota town surrounded on three sides by an iron mine began relocating about two hundred buildings two miles south in 1919, a gothic church in Most in the Czech Republic was moved half a mile in 1975 after the historic center was demolished for a lignite mine, and Chuquicamata in northern Chile was dismantled with residents relocated about nine miles to Calama to escape open-pit copper mine pollution.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A century-long pattern across iron, lignite and copper — town relocation is a recurring and predictable cost of long-life extraction, not a Swedish anomaly.

insights.claim: A local history teacher publicly rejects the dominant origin story, arguing that saying Kiruna's history begins with the railway and LKAB is glaringly obvious revisionist history because the site where the church was relocated used to be a resting place for reindeer.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Indigenous prior claims are the live contestation point for the rare-earth expansion, and they are already being voiced publicly by locals, not just activists.
insights.quote: Sometimes we misrepresent history and say the story begins when the railway and LKAB popped up here. That’s just nonsense. And a glaringly obvious revisionist history.

insights.claim: Residents systematically conceal dissatisfaction about the changes forced on the city, with one eighty-year-old woman being told she was lucky to have money from selling her flat and responding that she did not want money, she just wanted to live there.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Cash compensation does not clear the welfare loss and suppressed grievance leaves no measurable opposition signal — social license can look intact right up until it fails.
